issues.item: Threat: Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively
issues.explanation: 'Irritability' is not a threat appraisal/perception item; it reflects arousal/behavioral dysregulation and fits better outside the Threat node. In this profile, the other Threat items are coherent terrorism-related hypervigilance/safety behaviors ('Scanning Exits', 'Back to Wall'), so this item is internally mismatched within the node and weakly aligned with the formulation in which Memory-linked threat should reflect perceived current danger rather than aggressive behavior.

vignette: Michael, a 33-year-old African American tailor, sought help after a series of traumatic events left him feeling lost and constantly on guard. His life had taken an unexpected turn when he witnessed a terrorist attack in his neighborhood last year. The event was so horrifying that he still struggles to remember parts of it. Michael described the scene as chaotic and confusing, with flashes of violence and sudden silence that seemed equally terrifying. Since the incident, Michael found himself spending long hours on his phone or playing games online to avoid thinking about what had happened. He also picked arguments at work, often creating drama just to distract himself from the lingering trauma. The constant need for distraction was a way to cope with the feelings of self-doubt and weakness that plagued him. Michael’s self-doubt intensified as he began to see himself as someone who couldn’t be trusted to make the right decisions. He felt like he no longer belonged anywhere, which led him to avoid making any future plans. This sense of not belonging was deeply tied to his fragmented memories. Sometimes, when he tried to recall what happened during the attack, he would feel completely numb, as if it had happened to a stranger. Other times, the memories replayed like an endless film, looping through his mind. The memory gaps and emotional numbness only deepened Michael’s feelings of weakness and doubt about himself. He often found himself scanning for exits as soon as he entered any room or building, feeling unsafe unless his back was against a wall where he could see everything happening around him. This hypervigilance made it difficult to focus on his work at the tailor shop, leading to several mistakes that further fueled his self-doubt. Michael’s occupation as a tailor provided a backdrop for many of these behaviors and triggers. He would often be distracted by intrusive thoughts while working with fabric or cutting patterns, causing him to lose track of time and make errors in his designs. His colleagues noticed the changes in his behavior but didn't fully understand what was driving them. Over time, Michael’s hypervigilance became a constant presence, and he found himself constantly on edge. This made it nearly impossible for him to engage with others or enjoy his work as he once did. He had come to believe that every unfamiliar sound or movement could signal danger, which only fueled his need to avoid any potential triggers. The culmination of these experiences led Michael to seek help. What frightened him most was the fear that he would never be able to return to a normal life and the constant worry about when the next threat might emerge. He hoped for a way to regain control over his thoughts, emotions, and actions, finding solace in knowing that there were strategies and support systems available to help him navigate through this challenging period. Michael’s journey had been marked by significant challenges, but he was beginning to see a path forward. His hope lay in understanding the connection between his experiences and the symptoms that developed as a result, ultimately aiming for a sense of belonging and self-assurance once more.
